newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel battling budget gap with Makams.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel battling budget gap with Makams.

text.p: The Bank of Israel is relying on its Makam short-term debt certificates as the chief weapon in countering the government's expansionary fiscal policy, the bank's monetary department said on Wednesday.

The bank said the value of Makam certificates held by the public grew to 18.7 billion shekels as of November, compared with 13.87 billion shekels at the end of 1995 and just 6.26 billion shekels at the end of 1994.
Makams are unlinked instruments, similar to Treasury bills and traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
The bank noted it had undertaken other absorptive measures including its dollar-shekel swap programme.

At the same time, the central bank noted it had sharply cut back the extent of monetary tenders to the commercial banks, which inject money into the economy. In November, the tenders amounted to just 1.9 billion shekels, against a peak of 18.3 billion shekels in December 1993.

All told, the Bank of Israel absorbed 30.17 billion shekels from the economy in the first 11 months of 1996, compared with 16.9 billion shekels for all of 1995. In 1994 and the three years prior, the central bank had injected money into the economy.

The bank said its policy had been dictated by the government's widening budget deficit, which this year is expected to reach as much as four percent of gross dosmetic product, as well as its growing reliance on foreign borrowing to finance it.
The bank conceded that high interest rates had exacerbated the problem by spurring an inflow of foreign capital by private sector borrowing.
